steps.text: Print displays the words inside the quotation marks. Edit those words while keeping the quotation marks and parentheses.
This assigns three to the name goals. Later lines can use that name to look up its value.
This assigns five to attempts. Every attempt counts, whether it scores or misses.
Divide goals by attempts, then multiply by one hundred. Store the percentage in rate.
Print displays a label, the value of rate, and a percent sign. The label helps explain what the number means.
Shots is a list of five invented attempts. Each one means a goal; each zero means a miss. Commas separate the items.
Sum adds the list values. Because each goal contributes one and each miss contributes zero, this counts goals.
Len counts every item in the list, including zeros. This gives the total number of attempts.
Divide the goal count by the attempt count and multiply by one hundred to calculate the percentage.
Print displays the number of goals with its label.
Print displays the number of attempts with its label.
Round with the number one displays the rate to one decimal place. Print adds a label and percent sign.
This independent experiment starts with the original five attempts. It does not copy your previous round’s edit.
Sum adds the values and stores the goal count under goals, with an s.
Len counts the attempts, including missed shots.
This starter deliberately uses goal without an s. No value has been assigned to that name, so Python raises a name error. Compare it with goals above, repair the spelling, and run again.
After the earlier error is repaired, this line can print the goal count.
This line prints the attempt count. Adding a new list item changes this count, too.
This prints the calculated percentage rounded to one decimal place. Compare it with the earlier experiment that replaced a result instead of adding an attempt.
Import loads Matplotlib’s plotting tools and names them p l t. This is supplied scaffolding you can use without memorizing it.
A line beginning with a hash is a comment for people. This reminds you how the shot records are encoded.
Near stores five invented attempts for the three meter group. Each list item records one attempt.
Far stores ten invented attempts for the nine meter group. A larger group can have more goals without a higher percentage.
Sum near counts its goals. Len near counts its attempts. Dividing these and multiplying by one hundred gives the near percentage.
Apply the same calculation to the far list. Each group uses its own number of attempts.
Print displays the three meter group’s goals, attempts, and rounded percentage. Keep all three numbers when you compare groups.
Print displays the same information for the nine meter group so the comparison is visible as text, too.
This comment marks the supplied plotting scaffold. Your experiment changes list data above it.
Bar draws the near and far rates in the same order as the three meter and nine meter labels.
The vertical axis runs from zero to one hundred. Keeping the full percentage scale helps you compare the bars.
This labels the vertical axis as goal rate in percent.
Show displays the chart built from this run. Check that the bar heights agree with the printed rates.
This loads the supplied plotting tools and gives them the short name p l t.
Experiment stores your title as text. Rename it to describe your planned data edit. A title alone does not change the results.
Baseline stores the original invented attempts. Keep this list unchanged so you have a comparison.
Test starts as a separate list with the same values. Make your one planned edit here after predicting and running the baseline.
Calculate the baseline percentage using its goals and attempts.
Calculate the test percentage using its own goals and attempts. Adding an item changes the number of attempts as well.
Print displays your experiment title.
Print displays the baseline goal count, attempt count, and rounded percentage.
Print displays your test’s goal count, attempt count, and rounded percentage. Use these actual numbers in your finding.
This comment marks the provided chart scaffold. You can use it without memorizing the drawing commands.
Draw two bars for the baseline and test percentages, in that order.
Keep the vertical axis between zero and one hundred for both bars.
Label the vertical axis as goal rate in percent.
Display the chart for this run. If you edit the code again, run again before describing the new result.
